query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive approach that separately calculates lattice and electronic thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr—by coupling machine‐learned force fields for phonon dynamics with DFT-based Boltzmann transport calculations for the electrons—will yield thermal conductivity estimates that are within 20% of experimental measurements (i.e. total conductivities of 10–17 W/(K m) at high temperatures and nearly equal lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K) and outperform prior methods that rely on conflated or Debye-temperature‐based approximations.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr alloy produced under controlled conditions (e.g. spark plasma sintering) with low oxygen contamination (<0.12 wt%) and a parallel set with 1 wt% oxygen to assess sensitivity.
generation.intervention: Application of the new predictive model that explicitly decouples the two heat transport channels: (a) using on‐the‐fly machine‐leared force fields to capture atomic-scale fluctuations and phonon scattering for lattice conductivity, and (b) employing DFT-based Boltzmann transport calculations to determine the electronic conductivity.
generation.conditions: Temperature range from approximately 100 K to 1200 K; experiments performed on samples with minimal oxygen contamination as well as on samples intentionally prepared with ~1 wt% oxygen.
generation.structural_mediator: Local force-constant and mass fluctuations at the atomic level that affect phonon scattering, and corresponding electronic band structure modifications that influence free electron transport.
generation.mechanism: By modeling the lattice dynamics with an ML-enhanced approach that captures complex force-constant fluctuations and decoupling the contribution of electrons via ab initio electronic structure calculations, the model avoids the conflation inherent in simpler Debye or linear mixture approximations. This separation allows a more precise prediction by accounting for the differing temperature dependences and scattering mechanisms of phonons and electrons.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict lattice thermal conductivity and electronic thermal conductivity separately such that their sum matches experimental values (10–17 W/(K m) at high temperatures) with error margins less than 20% across the 100–1200 K range, and will specifically reflect the nearly equal contributions observed below 200 K in defect-free samples.
generation.baseline: Earlier approaches based on Debye temperature estimates and linear combination rules, which do not distinguish between lattice and electronic contributions and show larger deviations from measured conductivities.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold for single-phase, well-controlled HfNbTaTiZr specimens. It may break down in conditions where additional defect scattering or phase separation occurs (e.g., high oxygen contamination beyond 1 wt% or non-equilibrium microstructures).
generation.uncertainty: While the approach is expected to improve accuracy by roughly 20% over earlier models, uncertainties remain regarding the exact influence of oxygen on both phonon and electronic scatterings and the model’s transferability to samples with subtle microstructural variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one with minimal oxygen contamination (<0.12 wt%) and one with controlled 1 wt% oxygen. Measure the total thermal conductivity as well as identify separate lattice and electronic contributions using combined techniques (e.g., phonon spectroscopy for lattice dynamics and electrical resistivity measurements coupled with the Wiedemann–Franz law for electronic contributions) over the temperature range of 100–1200 K.
measurements: Phonon spectra/heat capacity to extract lattice thermal conductivity
Electrical resistivity and derived electronic conductivity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predictive model’s separate estimates for lattice and electronic contributions do not sum to within 20% error of the experimentally measured total conductivity over the full temperature range, or if the predicted equal contributions below 200 K are not observed in defect-free samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Extreme chemical complexity is one of the key features of these concentrated (particularly equiatomic) high entropy alloys. Their unique properties have been generally discussed from perspectives of alloy complexity, where the controlling factors are the number and the type of elements comprising the alloys. For example, the diffusion activation energy has been reported to be positively related to the number of elements in the matrix, while the hardening effect of HEAs (e.g. NiCoFeCrMn) has been considered to result from size/modulus mismatch between the alloying elements; in this case, certain alloying species (e.g. Cr) are more critical than the number of elements. In the case of physical properties, however, the general picture of the effects of chemical complexity on magnetism and electrical and thermal transport, especially at low temperatures, is still unclear in this new family of alloys. Moreover, considering the fact that CPA does not include the displacement fluctuation, whether or not it can capture the major feature of the transport properties in these compositionally complex alloys remains to be explored. HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy was produced by various methods of powder metallurgy including mechanical alloying, sintering, hot isostatic pressing, spark plasma sintering, and high pressure torsion. The microstructure and mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr prepared by various methods were examined. It was found that the main problem in fabrication of HfNbTaTiZr alloy by powder metallurgy is oxygen contamination. Samples prepared by cold isostatic pressing followed by sintering and/or hot isostatic pressing contained oxygen in the concentration range of 0.55 wt %–0.85 wt %. Oxygen contamination of samples prepared by mechanical alloying was even higher, and the oxygen concentration in these samples exceeded 1 wt %. Oxygen incorporated into the HfNbTaTiZr samples caused deterioration of mechanical properties (embrittlement) and prevented formation of a single phase random solid solution. Investigations performed in the present work showed that the most promising powder metallurgy method of production of HfNbTaTiZr alloy was spark plasma sintering of gas atomized powder. The difficulty of modeling phonon linewidths in random alloys comes from the complexity of taking into account the quoted three ingredients, i.e. atomic size, mass, and force-constant fluctuations. A simple analytical model, successfully used in mass disordered alloys, assumes phonon scattering from isolated defects and leads to the expression ΓFWHM = π/2(ℏω)2g(ℏω)〈ϵ2〉, where g(ℏω) is the GVDOS and ϵ represents the sum of all kinds of fluctuations contributions. Using this model, we find that the expected broadening from mass fluctuations in our HEA is negligibly small, at most 0.2 meV. Ascribing the whole observed linewidth to force-constant fluctuations, the global behavior is reproduced quite well along the [ζ00] direction using an average force-constant fluctuation ϵ = 〈ΔFij/Fij〉 ~ 20% (see Fig. 7). However, the agreement does not hold in all directions: the observed anisotropy then calls for more complex models. We therefore turn to the recent theoretical work of Mu et al..
